Geometric solids

Tin can, tower roof, shoebox, tent: all around us there are cylinders, pyramids, cuboids and prisms. In this chapter you describe solids precisely, draw them from the front, from above and as an oblique drawing, fold their nets and calculate volume and surface area – also for composite solids and prisms.

20 LESSONS4 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise solids and describe them with vertices, edges and faces
  • represent solids in a plan view, in side views, as an oblique drawing and as a net
  • calculate the volume and surface area of cuboids and of solids made up of cuboids
  • calculate the volume of right prisms with $V = G \cdot h$

$5 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 30$

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1Solids around us

A tin can has two circles and a curved wall: a cylinder. A pointed tower roof with a square ground plan is a pyramid. A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces.

Solids with only flat faces are also called polyhedra: cubes, cuboids, prisms, pyramids. Cylinders, cones and spheres have curved surfaces.

A prism has two identical, parallel bases and rectangles as its side faces. A cuboid is a special prism.

KEY POINT · VERTICES, EDGES, FACES

Cube and cuboid: 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces

Triangular prism: 6 vertices, 9 edges, 5 faces   ·   square pyramid: 5 vertices, 8 edges, 5 faces

Sphere: no vertex, no edge   ·   cone: one apex, one edge

Euler’s formula: for polyhedra, vertices + faces − edges = 2. Cube: $8 + 6 - 12 = 2$.

Dice: the numbers on opposite faces add up to 7.

INTERACTIVE · LOOKING AT A CUBOID

Change the edge lengths. Count the vertices, edges and faces. Which edges are equal in length and parallel?

EXAMPLE 1 · COUNTING A PRISM

How many vertices, edges and faces does a prism with a pentagon as its base have?

Vertices: $2 \cdot 5 = 10$. Edges: 5 at the bottom, 5 at the top, 5 vertical = 15. Faces: 2 pentagons + 5 rectangles = 7.

10 vertices, 15 edges, 7 faces – check: $10 + 7 - 15 = 2$ ✓

EXAMPLE 2 · GEOMETRY IN YOUR HEAD

A cube made of 27 small cubes (3 × 3 × 3) is painted red on the outside. How many small cubes have three red faces?

Only the cubes at the corners have three red faces.

8 cubes – along the edges, 12 cubes have two red faces, in the middle of the faces 6 have one, and 1 inside has none.

EXERCISES

Which solid? a) tin can   b) ice-cream cone   c) football   d) chocolate box with a triangle at the front and back   e) shoebox

a) cylinder   b) cone   c) sphere   d) triangular prism   e) cuboid

How many edges of a cuboid are just as long as a particular edge? How many edges meet at a vertex?

Three more (four equal, parallel edges). 3 edges meet at every vertex.

On a dice, the 2 is on top and the 3 at the front. Which numbers are at the bottom and at the back?

Bottom $7 - 2 = 5$, back $7 - 3 = 4$.

A prism has a 20-sided polygon as its base. How many vertices, edges and faces does it have? Check with Euler’s formula.

40 vertices, 60 edges, 22 faces. $40 + 22 - 60 = 2$ ✓

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a triangular prism have?

3 at the bottom, 3 at the top, 3 in between: 9

How many vertices does a pyramid with a square base have?

4 at the bottom and the apex: 5

A 3 × 3 × 3 cube painted on the outside: how many small cubes have no paint at all?

Only the one in the middle: 1

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2Views, oblique drawing and net

From above, a cylinder looks like a circle, from the front like a rectangle. So a single view is often not enough to recognise a solid. That is why you draw a plan view (from above) and side views – or an oblique drawing, which looks three-dimensional.

In an oblique drawing you draw the front face in its true size. The edges going back run at a slant of 45° and are shortened to half. Hidden edges are dashed.

A net is what you get when you cut open the surface of a solid and lay it out flat. A cube has 11 different nets.

KEY POINT · REPRESENTING

Plan view: view from above · Front view and side view: from the front and from the side

Oblique drawing: front in true size, going back at 45° and half as long, hidden edges dashed

Net: all the faces connected in the plane; folded up, it gives the solid

Not a net of a cube: six squares in a row, or a block of 2 × 3 squares.

Building plan: the numbers in the plan view say how many cubes are stacked there.

INTERACTIVE · SOLIDS MADE OF CUBES

Choose a solid or build your own: tap the cells in the building plan. The views from the front and from the right appear straight away.

INTERACTIVE · THE NET OF THE CUBOID

Switch to “Net”: which rectangles appear twice?

EXAMPLE 3 · OBLIQUE DRAWING

A cuboid is 4 cm wide, 3 cm deep and 2 cm high. How long do you draw the edges?

The front, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high, in true size. The depth of 3 cm at 45° and halved.

depth edges 1.5 cm long

EXAMPLE 4 · WHICH SOLID?

From the front a solid looks like a triangle, from above like a circle. Which one is it?

Round from above, pointed at the top.

a cone

EXERCISES

Draw the oblique drawing of a cube with an edge length of 4 cm. How long are the depth edges?

2 cm, going back at 45°. Three edges at the back, bottom left, are hidden and are dashed.

Which faces make up the nets of a) a cuboid   b) a triangular prism   c) a square pyramid   d) a cylinder?

a) 6 rectangles   b) 2 triangles, 3 rectangles   c) 1 square, 4 triangles   d) 2 circles, 1 rectangle

A solid made of cubes has the building plan: back 0, 0, 0 · middle 3, 2, 1 · front 3, 2, 1. How many cubes are there? Draw the front view.

12 cubes. From the front you see three columns with 3, 2 and 1 squares.

Draw three different nets of a cube and one shape made of six squares that is not a net of a cube. Explain why it does not work.

For example a cross (1-4-1), a staircase (2-2-2) and two offset rows of three (3-3). Not a net: six squares in a row – four form a ring, the fifth and sixth faces land on the first and second, and the top and bottom stay open.

TEST YOURSELF!

Depth 3 cm: how long do you draw the depth edge in the oblique drawing?

$3 : 2 = 1.5$

How many different nets of a cube are there?

11

Building plan middle 3, 2, 1 and front 3, 2, 1: how many cubes?

$6 + 6 = 12$

UNIT 35 LESSONS

3Volume and surface area of composite solids

A box of 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm holds exactly 24 centimetre cubes: 12 in one layer, 2 layers. That is its volume: 24 cm³. The surface area is the cardboard you need for the box.

Composite solids are calculated like composite shapes: split them into cuboids and add, or complete them to a large cuboid and subtract.

For the surface area, only the faces on the outside count. If two cubes are glued together, the two glued faces disappear.

KEY POINT · CUBOID

Volume: $V = a \cdot b \cdot c$   ·   Surface area: $O = 2 \cdot (a \cdot b + a \cdot c + b \cdot c)$

Cube: $V = a \cdot a \cdot a$, $O = 6 \cdot a \cdot a$

Units: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre · 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1000 litres

A feel for sizes: a shoebox holds about 8 litres, a classroom about 170 m³ of air.

Doubled edges: if all the edges are doubled, the volume becomes eight times as big.

INTERACTIVE · UNIT CUBES

Switch to “Unit cube” and change the edges. Count the cubes in one layer and the layers.

EXAMPLE 5 · AQUARIUM

An aquarium is 80 cm long, 40 cm wide and 50 cm high. How many litres does it hold?

In dm: $8 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 160$ dm³.

160 litres

EXAMPLE 6 · COMPOSITE

A cuboid of 4 cm × 8 cm × 2 cm is sawn out of a block of wood (10 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm). How much wood is left?

Whole block 400 cm³, sawn out 64 cm³.

336 cm³

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume and the surface area: a) cuboid 5 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm   b) cube with a 3 cm edge

a) 30 cm³ and 62 cm²   b) 27 cm³ and 54 cm²

A classroom is 8 m long, 7 m wide and 3 m high. How much air is in it?

168 m³ = 168,000 litres

A stair landing consists of two cuboids: 60 cm × 30 cm × 20 cm and 60 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm. How big is its volume in dm³?

$36{,}000 + 72{,}000 = 108{,}000$ cm³ = 108 dm³

Two cubes with a 2 cm edge are glued together. How big is the surface area of the new solid?

$2 \cdot 24 - 2 \cdot 4 = 40$ cm² (cuboid 4 × 2 × 2).

A present (30 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm) is wrapped. For overlaps you allow 10% more paper. How much paper do you need?

Surface area $2 \cdot (600 + 300 + 200) = 2200$ cm², with 10% more: 2420 cm².

TEST YOURSELF!

Surface area of the cuboid 5 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm in cm²?

$2 \cdot (15 + 10 + 6) = 62$

An aquarium of 80 cm × 40 cm × 50 cm: how many litres?

$8 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 160$

Two cubes with a 2 cm edge glued together: surface area in cm²?

$48 - 8 = 40$

UNIT 45 LESSONS

4Right prisms

If you saw a cuboid diagonally, you get two identical triangular prisms. Each has half the volume. The volume of a prism depends only on the base and the height – as with the cuboid: layer upon layer.

In a prism, the base $G$ is a polygon, and the side faces are rectangles. The height $h$ is the distance between the base and the top face. If the prism is lying down, the “height” is its length.

The side faces together are called the lateral surface. Unrolled, it is a rectangle as wide as the perimeter of the base and as high as the prism.

KEY POINT · PRISM

Volume: $V = G \cdot h$

Lateral surface: $M = u \cdot h$ ($u$ = perimeter of the base)   ·   Surface area: $O = 2 \cdot G + M$

The base first: it is often a triangle or a trapezium. You know its formula from chapter 3.2.

Tents and roofs are triangular prisms lying down: the triangle at the front is the base.

INTERACTIVE · PRISMS AND THEIR NETS

Choose a prism and change the base edge and the height. Switch between the oblique drawing and the net.

EXAMPLE 7 · TENT

A tent: entrance 2 m wide and 1.5 m high (triangle), 3 m long. How much air is inside?

$G = 2 \cdot 1.5 : 2 = 1.5$ m², $V = 1.5 \cdot 3$

4.5 m³

EXAMPLE 8 · SURFACE AREA

A prism has a right-angled triangle with 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm as its base and is 10 cm high. How big is its surface area?

$G = 3 \cdot 4 : 2 = 6$ cm², $M = 12 \cdot 10 = 120$ cm², $O = 12 + 120$

132 cm²

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume: a) $G = 12$ cm², $h = 5$ cm   b) triangular prism with $g = 4$ cm, $h_\Delta = 3$ cm, length 6 cm   c) trapezium prism with $a = 6$ cm, $c = 4$ cm, height of the trapezium 3 cm, length 10 cm

a) 60 cm³   b) $6 \cdot 6 = 36$ cm³   c) $15 \cdot 10 = 150$ cm³

An attic has a triangular cross-section (8 m wide, 3 m high) and is 10 m long. How big is the roof space?

$G = 12$ m², $V = 120$ m³

A prism has a volume of 90 cm³ and a base of 15 cm². How high is it? What happens to the volume if you double the height?

$h = 6$ cm. With double the height, the volume doubles to 180 cm³.

A ditch is 100 m long, 4 m wide at the top, 2 m wide at the bottom and 1.5 m deep. How much soil was dug out? How many lorry loads is that if a lorry holds 15 m³?

$G = (4 + 2) \cdot 1.5 : 2 = 4.5$ m², $V = 450$ m³. $450 : 15 = 30$ loads.

TEST YOURSELF!

A tent with an entrance of 2 m × 1.5 m (triangle) and a length of 3 m: volume in m³?

$1.5 \cdot 3 = 4.5$

A prism with the triangle 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm (right-angled) and a height of 10 cm: surface area in cm²?

$12 + 120 = 132$

$V = 90$ cm³, $G = 15$ cm²: height in cm?

$90 : 15 = 6$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A paddling pool is 5 m long, 3 m wide and 1.2 m deep. How many litres of water does it hold?

18 m³ = 18,000 litres

One litre of juice is to go into a cuboid. Compare the cube 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm with the cuboid 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm: which needs less cardboard?

Cube 600 cm², cuboid 700 cm². The cube saves material.

A shipping container is about 6 m long, 2.4 m wide and 2.5 m high inside. At most how many boxes of 60 cm × 40 cm × 50 cm fit in if they all stand the same way round?

Lengthwise $600 : 60 = 10$, across $240 : 40 = 6$, upwards $250 : 50 = 5$: $10 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 300$ boxes.

EXCURSIONPUZZLING

Eleven nets of a cube among 35 hexominoes

Shapes made of several identical squares joined along whole sides are called polyominoes. The American mathematician Solomon Golomb gave them their name in 1953. From six squares there are 35 different shapes, the hexominoes.

Only 11 of the 35 hexominoes can be folded into a cube. You find them by trying systematically: six nets have a row of four squares, the other five do not. Nets that are turned or reflected do not count twice.

Try it yourself: In your mind, roll a cube over a net: on each cell a different face is at the bottom. If every face is hit exactly once, it is a net of a cube.

Source: Solomon W. Golomb, “Checker Boards and Polyominoes”, American Mathematical Monthly 61 (1954), talk in 1953; 35 hexominoes, 11 of them nets of a cube.
